opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting part is that the two halves cover each other's weaknesses.

Natural-language reasoning is how mathematicians actually think. When you read a paper or talk to someone at a whiteboard, the ideas are informal. There's intuition, analogy, "this looks like that other problem I've seen." Large language models have become surprisingly good at this. They can propose a strategy, sketch an argument, or recall a relevant lemma. The problem is that informal reasoning is very hard to check. A model can write something that sounds completely convincing and still have a subtle gap in step seven, and nobody notices until a human expert spends hours on it. At scale, you can't rely on that.

Lean is the opposite. It's a formal language where every step has to be justified down to the axioms, and a small trusted kernel checks it. If Lean accepts the proof, it's correct. There's no "trust me." But writing Lean directly is painful. It's verbose, the libraries are huge, and the search space is enormous if you have no high-level plan.

So when you combine them, the language side does the creative work: what's the idea, what's the decomposition, which lemmas might help. The formal side gives you ground truth. That changes the learning problem. A lot of AI progress happens in domains where you have a clean reward signal, like games or code with unit tests. Mathematics has been hard because "is this proof correct?" was a fuzzy, human-judged signal. With Lean the reward is binary and trustworthy. You can let a system try millions of things, keep what verifies, and learn from it without worrying that it's reward hacking its way to nonsense.

There's also a bigger picture. If we want AI systems we can rely on, in math, software verification, or eventually anywhere correctness really matters, we need more than fluent outputs. We need outputs that come with guarantees. Math is the cleanest place to build that: reasoning that is both creative and verifiable. I think that combination is a step toward AI you don't just believe but can actually check.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that it comes from a frustration I had as a mathematician before I ever thought about it as an AI problem.

When you're doing research mathematics, there are really two very different activities happening at once. One is the creative, intuitive, language-based part: you're reading papers, you're forming conjectures, you have a hunch that two objects are secretly the same thing, you sketch an argument on a whiteboard. That's messy and verbal and full of "it should follow that" and "by a standard argument." The other activity is verification, where you actually have to make every step hold up. And in practice, mathematicians spend an enormous amount of time on the second part, and we're not even very good at it. Papers have gaps. Referees miss things. There are famous results that sat in the literature for years with errors.

Large language models, as they exist today, are extraordinary at the first activity and almost structurally unreliable at the second. They can produce something that reads exactly like a proof, with the right rhythm and the right vocabulary, and have a subtle hole in the middle. And crucially, they can't tell. The model's confidence doesn't track correctness. For a lot of applications you can tolerate that, but mathematics is the one domain where a 95% correct proof is worth nothing. It's binary.

That's what makes Lean so interesting to pair with it. Lean is a proof assistant where the kernel will simply refuse to accept a step that doesn't follow. So you get this very clean division of labor. The language model does what it's good at: proposing ideas, decomposing a problem, guessing which lemma might be useful, drawing on the intuition it has absorbed from reading all of human mathematics. And Lean does what it's good at, which is being an incorruptible referee. When the model is wrong, it finds out immediately, and it finds out exactly where it went wrong.

And then the part I find genuinely exciting is what that feedback loop does over time. In most domains, if you want to improve a model with reinforcement learning, you need a reward signal, and the reward signal is usually some human judgment or some proxy that can be gamed. Here the reward is perfect. The proof checks or it doesn't. There's no way to flatter the verifier. So you can let the system search, fail, learn from exactly how it failed, and try again, millions of times, without a human in the loop and without the risk that it's learning to produce things that merely sound right. Mathematics becomes one of the very few places where you can scale up self-improvement and actually trust what comes out the other side.

So for me it's two things at once. It's a practical route to systems that can do real mathematics rather than imitate it. And it's a kind of laboratory for a bigger question about AI, which is how you build systems that are both creative and correct, instead of having to choose.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that they bring complementary strengths. In natural language, you can explore an idea, draw an analogy, or sketch why something ought to be true without spelling out every detail. That flexibility is very useful for discovering a proof. But it also makes it easy to overlook a gap—to say, “Clearly this follows,” when that step is actually doing all the work.

Lean gives you a precise way to check those steps. You write down the statement and the proof, and its kernel checks whether the proof establishes the statement. That doesn’t tell you whether you formalized the question you intended, but it gives you a much firmer basis for trusting the reasoning once the statement is right.

So the exciting possibility is a feedback loop: the AI proposes an argument, tries to formalize it, and uses the failures to revise its reasoning. You’re combining a flexible way to search for ideas with a rigorous way to check them.

sol-6.1.text:
What interests me is that they bring complementary strengths. Language is a flexible way to explore a problem: you can draw analogies, propose a strategy, or explain why something should be true. But a convincing explanation can still have a gap. Lean gives you a way to make those steps precise and check whether they actually follow.

So you can imagine a loop where an AI develops an argument in natural language, tries to formalize it in Lean, and uses the feedback to revise its reasoning. The exciting part is that correctness becomes something the system can check, rather than just something its answer appears to have. That doesn’t make finding a proof easy, but it gives exploration a much firmer foundation.
